text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in Norwegian papers this morning:
- The state will have to spend at least one billion crowns to change computer systems before 2000. For many government departments, the turn of the century will have almost catastrophic consequences.

- A big mistake by goal keeper Joern Jamtfall was the beginning of the end for Trondheim's Rosenborg in the second leg match against Juventus in the quarter finals of the European Champions League. But Jamtfall soon turned his game round and was one of the team's best players on the night. Rosenborg lost 0-2 to the Italian champions.

- Shareholders in the Norwegian club in London Norway House will probably sell the building to an Israeli bank. In the heart of London near Trafalgar Square, the club has occupied Norway House since 1924.
- The police economic crime division will start an investigation into software house Sysdeco Group. The investigation will look into whether the company knowingly filed false accounts for 1995.

- Norwegian central bank chief Kjell Storvik is concerned that private consumption is increasing faster than expected. Norges Bank said on Wednesday that fresh economic forecasts pointed to continued moderate price inflation, but there was still a risk of an acceleration in price and wage inflation. It forecast consumer price inflation at 2.75 percent to 3.0 percent in 1997.

- The state will receive 3.5 billion crowns in dividend for 1996 from the two bank investment funds. In addition, the state is sitting on unrealised gains of 10.5 billion crowns from its shareholdings in Den norske Bank and Christiania Bank og Kreditkasse.

- Broker house Alfred Berg is recommending to investors technology company SuperOffice. The company was listed on the Oslo bourse's small and medium size caps list just over a week ago. In 1996 it had a deficit of two million crowns, but Alfred Berg says SuperOffice could book a profit of 50 million crowns in 1999.
